title: Military coup in Sudan
summary: Sudan's army dissolved the civilian-led transitional government and detained Prime Minister Abdalla Hamdok, ending the power-sharing arrangement agreed after the 2019 revolution.
body:
On 25 October 2021 the Sudanese military, led by General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, took control of the government. Prime Minister Abdalla Hamdok and other senior civilian officials were detained, the Sovereignty Council was dissolved and a state of emergency was declared. Al-Burhan blamed political infighting and said the takeover was needed to avoid civil war, according to the BBC.

The coup ended the power-sharing arrangement between the military and civilian groups that had been agreed in 2019, after mass protests led the army to remove Omar al-Bashir, who had ruled since 1989. Civilian groups including the Sudanese Professionals Association and the Forces of Freedom and Change called for civil disobedience, and protesters blocked roads in Khartoum and other cities. Security forces opened fire on demonstrators; at least 10 people were reported killed on the first day.

The African Union suspended Sudan's membership, and the United States and the World Bank suspended aid. Under pressure, al-Burhan reinstated Hamdok on 21 November 2021 under a 14-point agreement, but the main civilian coalitions rejected it and protests continued. Hamdok resigned on 2 January 2022 after failing to restore civilian rule.

The military's rule left unresolved the question of how the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, would be merged into the army. That dispute led to the war that broke out between the two forces in April 2023.

title: War in Sudan
summary: A war between Sudan's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, which began in Khartoum in April 2023, has displaced more than 14 million people and caused famine, according to the UN and other monitors.
body:
Fighting broke out in Khartoum on 15 April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), led by General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti. The two had seized power together in the 2021 coup, but fell out over how and when the RSF would be integrated into the army.

The RSF quickly took much of the capital, and the army-led government moved to Port Sudan on the Red Sea. By late 2023 the RSF controlled most of Darfur and had pushed into Gezira state. The army regained ground from 2024 and retook Khartoum in March 2025, while the RSF besieged El Fasher, the army's last stronghold in Darfur, and captured it in October 2025. Talks hosted in Jeddah by Saudi Arabia and the United States in 2023, and later mediation efforts, did not produce a lasting ceasefire.

The UN has described Sudan as the world's largest humanitarian emergency: its agencies estimated that 33.7 million people would need aid in 2026. More than 14 million people had been displaced by mid-2026, according to figures compiled on Wikipedia, and famine has been confirmed in several areas. Both sides have been accused of abuses; the United States determined in January 2025 that the RSF and allied militias had committed genocide in Darfur. Several countries have been accused of supplying the warring parties, including the United Arab Emirates, which denies arming the RSF.

In 2025 the RSF and its allies set up a rival administration, the Government of Peace and Unity, raising fears that the country could be split. The army-aligned government announced its return to Khartoum in January 2026, but drone strikes and fighting in Darfur and Kordofan continued.

title: M23 rebel offensive in eastern DR Congo
summary: The M23 rebel group, which UN experts say is backed by Rwanda, renewed its insurgency in eastern DR Congo in 2022 and in 2025 captured Goma and Bukavu, the two largest cities of the Kivu provinces.
body:
The March 23 Movement (M23), a rebel group first active in 2012–2013, resumed attacks on the Congolese army in North Kivu in late 2021 and launched a sustained offensive in March 2022, taking the border town of Bunagana in June. The Democratic Republic of the Congo accused Rwanda of invading its territory. Reports commissioned by the UN Security Council found that Rwanda armed and directed the group and that thousands of Rwandan soldiers fought alongside it; Rwanda denied backing M23 and accused Kinshasa of working with the FDLR, a Hutu rebel group formed in Congo by Rwandan exiles.

Regional forces from the East African Community and later the Southern African Development Community were deployed, and the Congolese government armed local militias known as Wazalendo. In January 2025 M23 captured Goma; the UN said at least 700 people were killed in five days of fighting there. The rebels took Bukavu in February.

The United States brokered a declaration of principles between DR Congo and Rwanda in April 2025 and a peace agreement in June, and Qatar mediated talks between Kinshasa and M23. Fighting continued: in December 2025 M23 took the city of Uvira, and US officials accused Rwanda of violating the agreement. The conflict has displaced hundreds of thousands of people, and human rights groups have documented abuses by M23 and other armed groups.

title: Genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda
summary: Over about 100 days in 1994, Hutu extremist militias and soldiers killed hundreds of thousands of Tutsi, as well as moderate Hutu and Twa, in one of the worst mass killings of the 20th century.
body:
The genocide began on 7 April 1994, the day after President Juvénal Habyarimana was assassinated. Hutu extremists in the army, the interim government and militias used the power vacuum to kill Rwanda's Tutsi minority and Hutu leaders seen as moderate. Victims were often killed by neighbours, and sexual violence was widespread.

The killing grew out of decades of ethnic tension, including the Hutu revolution of 1959–1962 that drove many Tutsi into exile, and the civil war that began in 1990 when the Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF), a mainly Tutsi rebel army, invaded from Uganda. A peace agreement, the Arusha Accords, had been signed in 1993. Estimates of the dead vary: Rwanda's constitution puts the toll at over one million, the BBC and Al Jazeera have cited around 800,000, and most scholarly estimates of Tutsi deaths range from about 500,000 to 662,000.

The UN and foreign powers did not intervene to stop the killing. The RPF, led by Paul Kagame, took Kigali on 4 July and ended the genocide by mid-July. A Rwanda-commissioned report published in 2021 concluded that France bore significant responsibility for enabling the genocide. The UN-backed International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda later convicted organisers including Théoneste Bagosora.

The perpetrators and many Hutu refugees fled into Zaire, now the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where they regrouped in camps along the border. This set off the First and Second Congo Wars and armed conflict in the Kivu provinces that continued for decades, including the M23 rebellions.

title: Mali War and the jihadist insurgency in the Sahel
summary: A conflict that began with a Tuareg rebellion in northern Mali in 2012 grew into a jihadist insurgency across the Sahel, outlasting a French intervention, UN peacekeepers and three military coups.
body:
In January 2012 Tuareg rebels of the National Movement for the Liberation of Azawad (MNLA), allied at first with jihadist groups including Ansar Dine and al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb, rose up in northern Mali. Soldiers angry at the government's handling of the rebellion overthrew President Amadou Toumani Touré in March, and the rebels took Timbuktu, Kidal and Gao within days. The MNLA declared an independent state of Azawad in April, which the African Union rejected; the jihadists then pushed the MNLA aside and took most of the north.

France intervened in January 2013 at the Malian government's request, and government forces retook most of the north. A UN peacekeeping mission, MINUSMA, was deployed, and the 2015 Algiers Accords sought to bring former rebels into the state. But jihadist violence spread into central Mali and neighbouring Burkina Faso and Niger. In 2017 several groups merged into Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), al-Qaeda's affiliate in the region, which has also fought an Islamic State affiliate.

Officers led by Assimi Goïta seized power in 2020 and again in 2021. The junta brought in Russian Wagner Group mercenaries, and France and its European partners announced their withdrawal in February 2022; MINUSMA left at the junta's request in 2023. Former Tuareg rebel groups returned to war and in 2024 merged into the Azawad Liberation Front (FLA).

In April 2026 JNIM and the FLA carried out coordinated attacks across the country, including in Bamako, took Kidal and, according to a military source quoted by Al Jazeera, killed the defence minister. The army, backed by Russia's Africa Corps, re-entered Kidal in October 2026.

title: Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger form the Alliance of Sahel States
summary: Three military-ruled Sahel countries formed a mutual defence pact in 2023 that became a confederation, left the West African bloc ECOWAS and turned from France and the West towards Russia.
body:
Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger signed the Liptako-Gourma charter on 16 September 2023, creating the Alliance of Sahel States (AES), a pact committing each to help the others, including militarily, if attacked. All three were ruled by military juntas that had taken power in coups between 2020 and 2023, most recently in Niger, where members of the presidential guard overthrew the elected president Mohamed Bazoum in July 2023 and installed General Abdourahmane Tchiani.

The three refused demands by the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) to restore democratic rule. They announced in January 2024 that they would leave the bloc, and their withdrawal took effect in January 2025. In July 2024 their leaders signed a confederation treaty in Niamey. The juntas cut military ties with Western powers: the United States completed its withdrawal from Niger in September 2024, and Russian forces replaced Western troops.

The confederation says it aims to pool resources, create a common market and currency, and eventually federate. Its members have expelled Western diplomats, downgraded the status of the French language and, in September 2025, announced their withdrawal from the International Criminal Court, which they called an instrument of neo-colonial repression. Amnesty International has accused AES governments of serious rights violations, and all three have postponed promised returns to civilian rule while jihadist insurgencies continue across the region.

title: Tigray War in northern Ethiopia
summary: A two-year war between Ethiopia's federal government, backed by Eritrea, and the Tigray People's Liberation Front, one of the deadliest conflicts of the century, ended with a ceasefire agreed in Pretoria in November 2022.
body:
The war began on 3 November 2020, when forces of the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which had dominated Ethiopian politics until Abiy Ahmed became prime minister in 2018, attacked federal army bases in Tigray. Abiy's government declared a state of emergency and launched what it called a law enforcement operation, with Eritrean troops attacking from the north. Federal forces took the regional capital, Mekelle, at the end of November.

Tigrayan forces fought on and retook Mekelle in June 2021, then pushed into the Amhara and Afar regions and, allied with the Oromo Liberation Army, advanced towards Addis Ababa, prompting a nationwide state of emergency in November 2021. A government counter-offensive pushed them back. A humanitarian truce declared in March 2022 collapsed in August, and fighting resumed until the federal government and the TPLF agreed a permanent cessation of hostilities on 2 November 2022, after talks in South Africa. Eritrea was not party to the deal.

The war caused famine and mass displacement. Estimates of the dead vary widely; the African Union mediator Olusegun Obasanjo has put the toll at about 600,000. In March 2023 the United States concluded that all sides had committed war crimes, including massacres, rape and ethnic cleansing.

Tensions remained over disputed Western Tigray and the TPLF's disarmament. In September 2026 the TPLF joined a new alliance of rebel groups, including Amhara Fano militias, and large-scale fighting resumed; federal forces re-entered Mekelle in early October 2026.

title: Fano insurgency in Ethiopia's Amhara region
summary: Amhara Fano militias, former allies of Ethiopia's government in the Tigray war, took up arms against it in 2023 after it moved to dissolve regional forces; the conflict has spread across much of the region.
body:
In April 2023 Ethiopia's government began dissolving the regional special forces as part of a plan to centralise the security services. In Amhara, the country's second-largest region, the move set off street protests and gun battles between local forces and the federal army, and some members of the special forces joined the Fano, loosely organised Amhara militias. Fano had fought alongside the government in the Tigray war but saw the 2022 peace deal with the Tigray People's Liberation Front as a betrayal.

In early August 2023 Fano fighters overran federal forces in several towns, including parts of Gondar, before the army pushed them back, and a state of emergency was declared at the regional government's request. Fighting spread through the Gondar and Gojjam zones in 2024; Fano now controls much of the countryside, while the army relies heavily on air and drone strikes. Rights groups have accused the army of extrajudicial killings, mass detentions and sexual violence, and extortion, theft and kidnapping have been widely reported in the countryside. Restrictions on communications and journalists have made the conflict hard to document; Wikipedia, citing reports, puts casualties at more than 15,000.

Ethiopia's government has accused Eritrea of arming Fano, which Eritrea denies. In September 2026 the Amhara Fano National Movement joined the Tigray People's Liberation Front, the Oromo Liberation Army and four other armed groups in an alliance pledged to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, shortly before large-scale fighting resumed in northern Ethiopia.

title: Islamist insurgency in Cabo Delgado, Mozambique
summary: An Islamic State-linked insurgency in Mozambique's gas-rich Cabo Delgado province has killed thousands of people and driven more than a million from their homes since 2017.
body:
The insurgency began on 5 October 2017 with an attack on the town of Mocímboa da Praia by Ansar al-Sunna, a local militant movement known to residents as al-Shabab, although it has no link to the Somali group of that name. The movement had emerged a few years earlier in the province's northern districts and drew fighters mainly from the area, along with some from Tanzania and Somalia. From 2019 the Islamic State claimed attacks in Mozambique, and in 2022 it declared a separate Mozambique Province.

The insurgents seized the port of Mocímboa da Praia in August 2020 and in March 2021 attacked the town of Palma, near a liquefied natural gas project led by TotalEnergies, which suspended work. Rwanda sent troops in July 2021, followed by a Southern African regional force, and Rwandan and Mozambican forces retook Mocímboa da Praia in August 2021. Attacks continued, targeting civilians as well as security forces.

TotalEnergies relaunched its $20bn gas project in January 2026; by then the fighting had killed more than 6,400 people, according to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project. A new wave of attacks from late 2025 reached all 17 districts of the province for the first time, and the UN says more than 1.3 million people have fled their homes during the conflict.

title: Boko Haram insurgency in north-east Nigeria and the Lake Chad region
summary: An Islamist uprising that began in Maiduguri in 2009 became one of Africa's longest wars, spreading from north-east Nigeria to Cameroon, Chad and Niger and splitting into rival Boko Haram and Islamic State factions.
body:
Boko Haram, a movement founded by the preacher Mohammed Yusuf in 2002 in opposition to Western education, launched an armed uprising in northern Nigeria in July 2009. About 150 people were killed in two days of fighting centred on Maiduguri, according to the BBC, and Yusuf was killed by Nigerian security forces. Under Abubakar Shekau the group regrouped and waged an insurgency marked by attacks on civilians, Muslims and Christians alike.

Violence peaked in 2014, when more than 10,000 people were killed according to figures compiled on Wikipedia and the group seized large areas of north-east Nigeria. In April 2014 it abducted about 276 schoolgirls from a secondary school in Chibok. In March 2015 Shekau pledged allegiance to the Islamic State; a Nigeria-led regional offensive that year pushed the militants back into the Sambisa Forest and around Lake Chad. The movement later split: a faction recognised by the Islamic State became Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), while Shekau's group kept the Boko Haram name. In May 2021 Nigerian officials said Shekau had died or been seriously wounded during clashes with ISWAP.

The insurgency has spread to Cameroon, Chad and Niger, and at one point closed about 57% of schools in Borno state, according to figures compiled on Wikipedia. Attacks continued in 2025 and 2026, including on Chadian troops on Lake Chad. In December 2025, after President Donald Trump accused Nigeria's government of failing to protect Christians, the United States carried out its first known strikes in Nigeria, against groups it said were linked to the Islamic State.

title: Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine
summary: Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022, escalating a conflict that began in 2014 into the largest war in Europe since the Second World War.
body:
In late 2021 Russia massed troops near Ukraine's borders and demanded guarantees from the West, including that Ukraine never join NATO. On 24 February 2022 President Vladimir Putin announced what he called a "special military operation", and Russian forces attacked from Belarus towards Kyiv, from occupied Crimea in the south and from the Donbas in the east. Ukraine declared martial law and ordered a general mobilisation.

Russian troops withdrew from around Kyiv by April 2022. Russia took Mariupol after a long siege, while Ukrainian counteroffensives in late 2022 retook most of Kharkiv region and the city of Kherson. In September 2022 Russia declared the annexation of four partly occupied regions after votes that Ukraine and its allies called a sham. The front then settled into a war of attrition, with Russia making slow gains in the Donbas, Ukraine mounting a cross-border incursion into Russia's Kursk region in August 2024, and both sides relying heavily on drones and long-range strikes.

According to Wikipedia's summary of available data, the war has caused hundreds of thousands of military casualties, Russian forces occupy roughly a fifth of Ukraine, and millions of Ukrainians have been displaced inside the country or have fled abroad. The UN reported that 2025 was the deadliest year for Ukrainian civilians since 2022. Many countries imposed sanctions on Russia and supplied Ukraine with aid, and the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Putin. US-brokered peace talks had not produced a settlement by 2026.

title: Russia annexes Crimea
summary: In February and March 2014 Russian forces seized Ukraine's Crimean peninsula, and Russia annexed it after a referendum held under occupation that Ukraine and most of the world rejected.
body:
The annexation followed the Revolution of Dignity in Kyiv, which ousted President Viktor Yanukovych on 22 February 2014. On 27 February armed men in uniforms without insignia began seizing strategic sites in Crimea, including the regional parliament, which then installed a pro-Russian government under Sergey Aksyonov and announced a referendum on the peninsula's status. Russia initially denied that the troops were its own; President Vladimir Putin later acknowledged that they were.

The referendum on 16 March was held under Russian occupation and offered no option to keep the existing status. The Russian-installed authorities reported an overwhelming vote to join Russia, and on 18 March Putin and Crimea's leaders signed a treaty absorbing the peninsula and the city of Sevastopol into Russia, telling parliament that Crimea had "always been part of Russia". Ukraine said it would never accept the treaty, and its remaining forces withdrew from the peninsula within days.

The UN General Assembly adopted a resolution affirming Ukraine's territorial integrity and rejecting the referendum. The other G8 members suspended Russia and imposed sanctions, and NATO suspended co-operation with Moscow. The annexation, the first by a European country of another's territory since the Second World War, is regarded as the start of the Russo-Ukrainian war, which escalated into a full-scale invasion in 2022.

title: Dissolution of the Soviet Union
summary: The Soviet Union formally ceased to exist on 26 December 1991, splitting into 15 independent states and ending the Cold War.
body:
By the late 1980s the Soviet Union faced chronic economic stagnation, the cost of the arms race and foreign wars, and rising nationalism in its 15 union republics. Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms of openness (glasnost) and restructuring (perestroika) loosened central control. Estonia declared state sovereignty in November 1988, and Lithuania became the first republic to declare independence, in March 1990.

In August 1991 communist hardliners attempted a coup against Gorbachev to reverse his reforms. It failed within days, but the central government lost authority and many republics declared independence. On 8 December 1991 the leaders of Russia, Belarus and Ukraine signed the Belovezha Accords, declaring that the Soviet Union no longer existed and creating the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS); most other republics joined on 21 December.

Gorbachev resigned on 25 December 1991 and handed his powers, including control of nuclear weapons, to Russian president Boris Yeltsin; the Soviet flag over the Kremlin was replaced by the Russian tricolour that evening. The next day the upper chamber of the Supreme Soviet formally dissolved the union. Russia became its recognised successor state. The new borders between the successor states, including Ukraine's, later became the focus of conflicts such as Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014.

title: Gaza war
summary: A war in Gaza and Israel that began with the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 and the Israeli offensive that followed; a US-backed ceasefire from October 2025 has not ended the violence.
body:
On 7 October 2023 Hamas led an attack on southern Israel in which 1,195 people, most of them civilians, were killed and 251 were taken hostage. Israel responded with an air campaign and, from 27 October, a ground invasion of the Gaza Strip, with the stated aims of destroying Hamas and freeing the hostages. Israeli forces fought in Gaza City, Khan Yunis and Rafah, and Israel killed Hamas leaders inside and outside Gaza.

According to the Gaza Health Ministry, more than 75,000 Palestinians had been reported killed by late September 2026; peer-reviewed studies suggest the ministry's count is an undercount, while Israel disputes the figures. Nearly all of Gaza's 2.3 million people were displaced and most of its infrastructure was destroyed. The IPC hunger monitor confirmed famine in Gaza Governorate in August 2025, a finding Israel's aid co-ordination body contested. A UN commission of inquiry concluded in September 2025 that Israel had committed genocide; Israel rejected the report as false, and a genocide case brought against Israel is before the International Court of Justice. Experts have also accused Hamas of war crimes.

Two ceasefires, in November 2023 and January 2025, allowed exchanges of hostages and Palestinian prisoners but broke down. A third ceasefire, the first phase of a 20-point US plan, took effect on 10 October 2025, and the last living hostages were released three days later. Israeli strikes have continued since, and disputes over Hamas's disarmament and Israel's withdrawal have slowed later phases of the plan. The war spread across the region, including fighting between Israel and Hezbollah in Lebanon and between Israel and Iran.

title: Civil war in Yemen
summary: A civil war between Yemen's Houthi movement and the internationally recognised government and its Saudi-led allies, which began when the Houthis seized Sanaa in 2014 and returned to full-scale fighting in 2026.
body:
The Houthis, a Zaydi Shia movement from northern Yemen, stormed the capital, Sanaa, in September 2014 after weeks of protests over fuel subsidy cuts. In January 2015 they seized the presidential palace, and President Abdrabbuh Mansur Hadi resigned, later withdrawing his resignation from Aden. In March 2015 a coalition of Arab states led by Saudi Arabia and backed by the US began air strikes to halt the Houthi advance and restore Hadi's government. The war is widely seen as part of the rivalry between Saudi Arabia and Iran, which backs the Houthis.

The Houthis kept control of Sanaa and most of the former North Yemen, while the government side split between Saudi-backed forces and southern separatists of the UAE-backed Southern Transitional Council (STC). According to the UN, more than 150,000 people were killed in fighting and many more died from hunger and disease; the UN has also said coalition air strikes killed tens of thousands of people. A UN-brokered truce from April 2022 brought relative calm, and in April 2022 a Presidential Leadership Council replaced Hadi.

In December 2025 the STC seized almost all of the south. Saudi-backed government forces retook it in January 2026, and the STC's leadership announced its dissolution in a move its spokesman rejected. In mid-2026, amid a regional war involving Iran, the Saudi–Houthi ceasefire collapsed: the Houthis declared a blockade of Saudi Arabia and in September launched an offensive that captured Mocha and the Bab al-Mandab strait and moved on Taiz. The UN envoy told the Security Council in October 2026 that Yemen had fallen back into full-scale war.

title: Arab Spring
summary: A wave of pro-democracy protests and uprisings that began in Tunisia in December 2010, toppled leaders in Tunisia, Egypt, Libya and Yemen, and led to civil wars in Syria, Libya and Yemen.
body:
On 17 December 2010 Mohamed Bouazizi, a street vendor in Sidi Bouzid, Tunisia, set himself on fire after police confiscated his produce. His death on 4 January 2011 fuelled nationwide protests over unemployment, the cost of living and repression, and President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali fled to Saudi Arabia ten days later after 23 years in power.

The protests spread across the Arab world under the slogan "the people want to bring down the regime". In Egypt, mass demonstrations centred on Cairo's Tahrir Square forced Hosni Mubarak to resign on 11 February 2011. In Libya, a crackdown on protests in Benghazi turned into a civil war in which French, British and US air forces intervened, and Muammar Gaddafi was killed in October 2011. Yemen's Ali Abdullah Saleh handed power to his deputy in February 2012. Protests in Bahrain were suppressed, and in Syria demonstrations that began in March 2011 were met with violent repression and became a civil war.

The first wave faded by 2012. Tunisia held its first free election in October 2011, but early hopes elsewhere gave way to repression and conflict: Egypt's elected president Mohamed Morsi was overthrown by the military in 2013, and wars in Syria, Libya and Yemen continued for years. A second wave of protests from 2018 brought down leaders in Sudan and Algeria.

title: Syrian civil war
summary: A war that grew out of the 2011 uprising against Bashar al-Assad, drew in regional and world powers and the Islamic State group, and ended with the fall of the Assad government in December 2024.
body:
In March 2011, as part of the Arab Spring, protests broke out in Syria against the rule of Bashar al-Assad, beginning in the southern city of Daraa. Security forces met them with lethal force, which UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon called unacceptable. Defections and armed opposition groups such as the Free Syrian Army followed, and the uprising became a civil war.

The opposition received support from Qatar, Turkey and the United States, while Iran, Hezbollah and, from 2015, Russia backed the government. Government forces used chemical weapons, most lethally in the sarin attack on Ghouta in August 2013. In 2014 the Islamic State group seized much of eastern Syria and western Iraq, prompting a US-led air campaign and support for the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces, which, with others, defeated the group territorially. Turkey intervened in the north from 2016. Government forces, backed by Russian air power, retook Aleppo in December 2016, and after an offensive on Idlib a ceasefire largely froze the front lines from 2020.

The war displaced millions of people; an estimated 6.7 million Syrians had fled the country by December 2022, according to figures cited on Wikipedia, with the largest number in Turkey. In late November 2024 rebels led by Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham launched an offensive from Idlib that took Aleppo within days, then Hama and Homs, while southern rebels advanced on Damascus. Assad fled to Moscow on 8 December 2024, ending more than 50 years of rule by his family. Many sources regard this as the end of the civil war, although clashes continued into 2026.

title: Fall of Assad and Syria's political transition
summary: After Bashar al-Assad fled in December 2024, a government led by former rebel commander Ahmed al-Sharaa began a five-year transition marked by outbreaks of sectarian violence and disputes with Kurdish and Druze groups.
body:
On 8 December 2024 an opposition offensive spearheaded by Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) reached Damascus, and Bashar al-Assad fled to Russia, where he was granted asylum. The collapse ended more than five decades of rule by the Assad family. A caretaker government took over, and in January 2025 HTS leader Ahmed al-Sharaa was named president for a transitional period, the constitution was suspended and armed factions were ordered to dissolve into state institutions.

In March 2025 al-Sharaa signed a provisional constitutional declaration setting a five-year transition with a strong presidency, and formed a transitional government of 23 ministers that included Alawite, Druze, Christian and Kurdish members. The transition was shaken by sectarian violence: in March 2025 clashes between security forces and Assad loyalists on the coast were followed by killings of hundreds of Alawite civilians, according to the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, and in July 2025 fighting between Druze and Bedouin groups and government forces in Suwayda left hundreds dead and drew Israeli air strikes.

Indirect parliamentary elections were held in October 2025, with electoral colleges choosing two-thirds of the People's Assembly and the president appointing the rest. In January 2026, after a government offensive against the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces, al-Sharaa declared a ceasefire, recognised Kurdish as a national language and restored citizenship to stateless Kurds. As of mid-2026 a Druze-led council controlled most of Suwayda governorate.

title: Earthquakes strike Turkey and Syria
summary: Two earthquakes of magnitude 7.8 and 7.5–7.7 struck southern Turkey and northern Syria on 6 February 2023, killing tens of thousands of people in the deadliest natural disaster in modern Turkish history.
body:
The first earthquake, of magnitude 7.8, struck at 04:17 local time on 6 February 2023 near Nurdağı, about 37 km west-north-west of Gaziantep and close to the Syrian border. About nine hours later a second major earthquake, measured at magnitude 7.5 by the US Geological Survey (7.7 in other estimates), struck about 95 km to the north-north-east. More than 30,000 aftershocks followed over three months. The quakes resulted from strike-slip faulting along the East Anatolian fault system.

Damage stretched across an area of about 350,000 square kilometres. Turkey's confirmed death toll was 53,537, and estimates of the dead in Syria ranged from about 6,000 to 8,500. UN development experts estimated that around 1.5 million people were left homeless. Damaged roads, winter storms and broken communications hampered rescue efforts, which drew more than 141,000 people from 94 countries after Turkey appealed for international help. In north-west Syria, the disaster hit a region where 4.1 million people already relied on humanitarian aid after years of war.

It was the deadliest earthquake in the area of present-day Turkey since the Antioch earthquake of 526 and the deadliest worldwide since the 2010 Haiti earthquake. Damage was estimated at about US$150 billion in Turkey, and a UN-backed assessment put Syria's recovery needs at almost US$15 billion. By the day after the first quake, more than 5,700 buildings in Turkey had collapsed, according to the country's disaster agency.

title: Mahsa Amini protests in Iran
summary: Nationwide protests under the slogan "Woman, Life, Freedom" broke out in Iran after Mahsa Amini died in the custody of the morality police in September 2022; they were suppressed by spring 2023.
body:
Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman from Saqqez, was arrested in Tehran by Iran's morality police (the Guidance Patrol) on 13 September 2022 for allegedly wearing her hijab improperly. Witnesses said she was beaten in custody, which the authorities denied. She collapsed, fell into a coma and died on 16 September.

Protests began in her hometown of Saqqez and spread across Iranian Kurdistan and the rest of the country, led in large part by women and students. Besides demanding more rights for women, many protesters called for an end to the Islamic Republic itself, which set the movement apart from earlier protests over elections or the economy. The government responded with internet blackouts, tear gas and live fire. Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei called the unrest "riots" planned by the United States and Israel. At least 551 people, including 68 minors, had been killed by mid-September 2023, according to figures cited on Wikipedia, and around 19,000 people were arrested; Iran also executed several protesters.

By spring 2023 the protests had largely subsided without changing the country's leadership. In February 2024 a UN fact-finding mission concluded that the authorities had committed crimes against humanity, and in September 2026 Amnesty International reported the same, adding that the crackdown on Iran's 2025–2026 protests showed similar features on a larger scale. Solidarity protests were held in many cities abroad.

title: Protests in Georgia over a disputed election and the halt to EU accession
summary: Near-daily protests in Georgia that began after the disputed October 2024 parliamentary election and grew when the governing Georgian Dream party suspended the country's EU accession process.
body:
Protests began in Tbilisi on 28 October 2024, two days after a parliamentary election that official results said the governing Georgian Dream party had won with about 54 percent of the vote. Opposition parties and President Salome Zourabichvili rejected the result as fraudulent, and the EU and the United States called for alleged irregularities to be investigated. Georgian Dream denied that the vote was rigged.

The movement grew sharply on 28 November 2024, when Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze announced that his government would suspend the EU accession process until the end of 2028. Demonstrators gathered nightly outside parliament on Rustaveli Avenue and in other cities. Police used water cannon, tear gas and pepper spray, and the country's public defender said injuries inflicted on detained protesters amounted to torture. Opposition leaders were detained or attacked, and in 2025 the government passed laws raising fines and detention terms for protest offences. The government described the protests as violent and accused foreign actors of backing them.

Georgian Dream's candidate, Mikheil Kavelashvili, was chosen president by an electoral college in December 2024 and sworn in on 29 December; Zourabichvili said she remained the only legitimate president. In February 2025 the European Parliament said it did not recognise the results of the parliamentary and presidential elections, and the United States, the United Kingdom and several EU states sanctioned Georgian officials.

On 4 October 2025, the day of local elections that the main opposition blocs boycotted, a group of protesters tried to force their way into the presidential palace and was pushed back by riot police; prosecutors charged five opposition figures with attempting to overthrow the government. Daily protests marked their first anniversary in November 2025 and continued into 2026, according to Wikipedia's account of the movement.

title: Student-led anti-corruption protests in Serbia
summary: Two years of student-led protests that began after a railway station canopy collapsed in Novi Sad in November 2024, killing 16 people, and ended when a student-backed list won the October 2026 election.
body:
On 1 November 2024 the concrete canopy of the recently renovated railway station in Novi Sad collapsed, eventually killing 16 people. The renovation had been carried out as part of a project with Chinese contractors, and protesters blamed corruption and a lack of transparency in public works for the deaths. Early vigils turned into larger demonstrations demanding the release of documents about the reconstruction and accountability for those responsible.

From 22 November, after students were attacked during a silent tribute in Belgrade, students blockaded university faculties across the country and became the movement's organisers. Protesters stopped traffic for 16 minutes each day in memory of the victims, and the protests spread to hundreds of towns. Prime Minister Miloš Vučević resigned in January 2025. On 15 March 2025 an independent monitor estimated that 325,000 people or more rallied in Belgrade, which the BBC described as Serbia's largest protest; the government put the figure at 107,000.

In 2025 the students called for early parliamentary elections. Clashes with police and with supporters of the governing Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) became more frequent, with dozens of arrests after a large rally in June and several nights of violence in August. President Aleksandar Vučić accused the protesters of being part of a foreign-backed attempt to topple the state and denied responsibility for the problems they raised.

In June 2026 Vučić said he would step down, and on 27 September 2026 he resigned and called a snap parliamentary election, which he contested as his party's candidate for prime minister. In the vote on 25 October 2026, with turnout near 70 percent, the Student List defeated Vučić's coalition and he conceded. Wikipedia's account of the movement dates the end of the protests to that election.

title: Explosion at the Port of Beirut
summary: About 2,750 tonnes of ammonium nitrate stored at Beirut's port exploded on 4 August 2020, killing at least 218 people, injuring thousands and devastating much of the Lebanese capital.
body:
On the evening of 4 August 2020 a fire at a warehouse in the Port of Beirut set off about 2,750 tonnes of ammonium nitrate. The chemical had been unloaded from the cargo ship MV Rhosus and confiscated in 2014, then stored at the port for six years without adequate safety measures, according to Lebanese officials and later investigations.

The blast killed at least 218 people, injured about 7,000 and left roughly 300,000 people displaced, with damage estimated at US$15 billion, according to figures compiled by Wikipedia. It destroyed much of the port, including part of its grain silos, damaged neighbourhoods across the city and was felt as far away as Cyprus. The US Geological Survey registered it as a seismic event of magnitude 3.3. The United Nations, whose peacekeepers were among the injured, said it was helping with the emergency response.

The explosion struck a country already in a deep economic crisis and struggling with the COVID-19 pandemic. Anger at officials accused of negligence and corruption brought renewed protests, and Prime Minister Hassan Diab's government resigned on 10 August 2020.

The judicial investigation, led by Judge Tarek Bitar, was repeatedly halted by legal challenges from politicians he sought to question and by opposition from Hezbollah and its allies, who called the inquiry biased; Hezbollah denied any link to the explosion. The investigation resumed in January 2025, and in August 2025 Lebanon's culture minister said the damaged silos would be listed as a historic monument.

title: Notre-Dame de Paris burns and is rebuilt
summary: A fire in April 2019 destroyed the spire and most of the roof of Notre-Dame de Paris; after five years of restoration funded by donations, the cathedral reopened in December 2024.
body:
On the evening of 15 April 2019 a fire broke out in the roof space of Notre-Dame de Paris, the medieval cathedral on the Île de la Cité, which is part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The spire was being restored at the time. The blaze destroyed the wooden spire, rebuilt in the 19th century, and most of the oak roof, and damaged the upper walls. The stone vaults largely held, and firefighters saved the two towers and the main structure; many relics and works of art were carried out to safety. The fire also spread toxic lead dust over the site and nearby areas.

Paris prosecutors said in June 2019 that an improperly extinguished cigarette or an electrical fault could have started the fire and found no sign of criminal intent. President Emmanuel Macron set a five-year deadline for the restoration, and the French parliament passed a law governing the work in July 2019. Donors pledged hundreds of millions of euros within days, and more than €840 million had been given by 2021.

The cathedral stayed closed for more than five years; in 2019 it held no Christmas Mass for the first time since 1803. As chief architect Philippe Villeneuve had urged, the roof and spire were rebuilt as they had been, with oak framing and lead, rather than to a modern design. General Jean-Louis Georgelin, who led the reconstruction, died during a mountain hike in August 2023 and was succeeded by Philippe Jost.

Notre-Dame reopened on 7 December 2024 at a ceremony attended by world leaders including Donald Trump and Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and its inaugural Mass followed the next day. Restoration of the surroundings and some interior fittings continued into 2026.

title: Azerbaijan takes Nagorno-Karabakh and its Armenian population flees
summary: A one-day Azerbaijani offensive in September 2023 forced the surrender of the breakaway Armenian-run Republic of Artsakh; within days nearly all of Nagorno-Karabakh's roughly 120,000 Armenians left for Armenia.
body:
Nagorno-Karabakh, internationally recognised as part of Azerbaijan, had been run by ethnic Armenian authorities since a war in the early 1990s. After the 2020 war Azerbaijan regained much of the surrounding territory, and from December 2022 it blockaded the region's only road link to Armenia, the Lachin corridor, leading to shortages of food and medicine.

On 19 September 2023 Azerbaijan launched what it called an "anti-terrorist" operation, shelling Stepanakert and other areas and demanding that Karabakh's forces disarm and dissolve their government. After about 24 hours the Armenian authorities agreed to a ceasefire mediated by Russian peacekeepers, and President Ilham Aliyev declared that Azerbaijan's sovereignty had been restored. On 28 September the region's leader, Samvel Shahramanyan, signed a decree dissolving its institutions by 1 January 2024.

From 24 September people fled along the Lachin corridor to Armenia. A fuel depot explosion near Stepanakert on 25 September killed at least 20 people, according to local officials. By the end of the month Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said more than 100,000 of the region's estimated 120,000 inhabitants had left. Pashinyan accused Azerbaijan of ethnic cleansing, and human rights groups and genocide-prevention experts warned of it; Azerbaijan denied this and said residents were free to stay or go. When a UN mission, the first in about 30 years, arrived on 1 October, nearly the entire Armenian population had already gone.

In November 2023 the International Court of Justice ordered Azerbaijan to allow those who had fled to return safely. The end of the Artsakh republic closed a conflict that had lasted more than three decades.

title: COVID-19 pandemic
summary: A pandemic of a new coronavirus, SARS-CoV-2, that began in Wuhan, China, in December 2019, spread worldwide in 2020 and caused millions of deaths and the deepest global recession since the Great Depression.
body:
In late December 2019 health authorities in Wuhan, China, reported a cluster of pneumonia cases, later traced to a new coronavirus, SARS-CoV-2. The disease it causes, COVID-19, spread across Asia and then the world in early 2020. The World Health Organization (WHO) declared a public health emergency of international concern on 30 January 2020 and described the outbreak as a pandemic on 11 March.

Governments responded with travel restrictions, lockdowns, school and business closures, mask mandates, testing and contact tracing. Mutations produced a series of variants that differed in how easily they spread and how severe the illness was. The pandemic caused the largest global recession since the Great Depression, disrupted supply chains and education, and made remote work far more common; it also fuelled misinformation and political conflict over public health measures.

Vaccines were developed at unprecedented speed. In November 2020 Pfizer and BioNTech reported that their vaccine was more than 90 percent effective in trials, and mass vaccination began in December 2020, supported for poorer countries by programmes such as COVAX.

The WHO declared on 5 May 2023 that COVID-19 was no longer a global health emergency, while warning that it remained a threat. By October 2026 about 7.1 million deaths had been confirmed, and estimates of the true toll range from about 18 to 35 million, according to figures compiled by Wikipedia. Experts generally regarded the disease as endemic by 2025. In May 2025 WHO member states adopted a Pandemic Agreement intended to improve preparedness for future pandemics.

title: Clade Ib mpox epidemic and global health emergency
summary: A new strain of mpox, clade Ib, spread from eastern DR Congo from 2023, leading the WHO to declare a global health emergency in August 2024; the emergency ended in 2025, but cases continued.
body:
Mpox, formerly called monkeypox, is a viral disease long endemic among small mammals in central Africa that can pass to people, causing fever and a blistering rash. A global outbreak of a milder strain in 2022 led the World Health Organization (WHO) to declare an emergency that lasted until May 2023.

From September 2023 cases of a new variant, clade Ib, grew in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, first noticed around the mining town of Kamituga in South Kivu. The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) said in August 2024 that the fatality rate was 3 to 4 percent, well above that of the 2022 outbreak, and that children accounted for most cases and deaths in the DRC. Cases spread to neighbouring countries, and travel-linked cases were reported further afield, including in Europe. Health workers warned of spread in refugee camps, where cholera, measles and malnutrition were already straining care.

Africa CDC declared a continental emergency on 12 August 2024 and the WHO declared a public health emergency of international concern two days later. Vaccine donations from the United States, Germany and the EU began to reach Africa in late August and September 2024, and in September the WHO prequalified the MVA-BN vaccine, the first against mpox, after criticism of slow deliveries.

On 5 September 2025 WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus ended the international emergency, citing sustained declines in cases in the DRC, Burundi, Sierra Leone and Uganda. Africa CDC kept its continental emergency in place, pointing to surges in other African countries. Clade Ib continued to spread into 2026, with local transmission reported in Spain in December 2025 and in Germany in early 2026, according to Wikipedia.

title: James Webb Space Telescope launches and begins observing the early universe
summary: The largest telescope ever put in space, built by NASA with the European and Canadian space agencies, launched on 25 December 2021 and has since observed the most distant galaxies known.
body:
The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) is an infrared observatory built by NASA in partnership with the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Canadian Space Agency. Its 6.5-metre primary mirror, made of 18 gold-coated beryllium segments, gives it about six times the light-collecting area of the Hubble Space Telescope. Because distant galaxies' light is stretched into the infrared, Webb can see objects too old, faint or distant for Hubble, as well as analyse the atmospheres of planets around other stars. Planning began in 1996; after long delays and cost overruns the project cost about US$10 billion.

Webb lifted off on an Ariane 5 rocket from Europe's Spaceport at Kourou, French Guiana, on 25 December 2021. Over the following weeks it unfolded its five-layer sunshield and its mirror, and on 24 January 2022 it entered orbit around the Sun–Earth L2 point, about 1.5 million kilometres from Earth. The precision of the launch left enough fuel for a mission that may last around 20 years, according to Wikipedia.

US President Joe Biden released Webb's first full-colour image, a deep field crowded with thousands of galaxies, on 11 July 2022, and science operations began the next day. Since then Webb has repeatedly broken the record for the most distant galaxy observed, found unexpectedly bright and massive galaxies and black holes in the early universe, and studied the atmospheres of exoplanets. Its results are reshaping models of how the first galaxies and black holes formed, and the mission continues.

title: India's Chandrayaan-3 lands near the Moon's south pole
summary: India's Chandrayaan-3 mission set its Vikram lander and Pragyan rover down near the lunar south pole on 23 August 2023, making India the fourth country to soft-land on the Moon and the first near its south pole.
body:
Chandrayaan-3 was the Indian Space Research Organisation's (ISRO) second attempt to land on the Moon, after the Vikram lander of Chandrayaan-2 crashed in September 2019. The region near the lunar south pole interests scientists because shadowed craters there are thought to hold ice, which could reveal the history of the Moon and the Solar System and could one day supply water, oxygen and fuel for crewed missions.

The spacecraft, made up of a propulsion module, the Vikram lander and the small Pragyan rover, was launched on an LVM3 rocket from Sriharikota on 14 July 2023 and entered lunar orbit on 5 August. Vikram touched down at about 69 degrees south on 23 August 2023. India became the fourth nation to make a soft landing on the Moon, after the Soviet Union, the United States and China, and the first to land near the south pole. Prime Minister Narendra Modi named the landing point Shiv Shakti and declared 23 August India's National Space Day.

Over about ten days the rover drove across the surface and its instruments made the first on-site measurements of soil composition near the south pole, confirming the presence of sulphur along with oxygen, aluminium, iron and other elements, according to ISRO. Vikram also briefly fired its engines to hop about 40 centimetres. Neither craft was designed to survive the lunar night: both were put to sleep in early September, and they did not respond to wake-up calls when sunlight returned on 22 September.

The propulsion module was later moved from lunar orbit back into a high orbit around Earth, and a NASA orbiter used a laser reflector on Vikram to locate it on the surface. Studies of the mission's data, including the effects of Vikram's hop on the lunar soil, were still being published in 2026. ISRO's former chairman K. Sivan put the mission's estimated cost at about ₹615 crore.

title: Fourth global coral bleaching event
summary: Record ocean heat from early 2023 to mid-2025 bleached reefs in more than 80 countries and territories, exposing 84% of the world's coral reef area to bleaching-level heat stress, the most extensive event on record.
body:
Corals bleach when water that is too warm for too long makes them expel the algae living in their tissues, which supply much of their food and their colour. Bleached corals can recover if temperatures fall, but prolonged or repeated heat kills them. Reefs cover less than 1 percent of the ocean floor but shelter about a quarter of marine species, and support fisheries, tourism and coastal protection. Three earlier global bleaching events were recorded in 1998, 2010 and 2014–2017.

From early 2023, record sea surface temperatures, which scientists attribute mainly to climate change and which coincided with 2024 becoming the hottest year on record, pushed reefs in all three tropical ocean basins into heat stress. Corals in the Florida Keys bleached in mid-2023 after water temperatures reached record highs, and reefs off Mexico's Pacific coast suffered heavy die-offs. The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) confirmed a fourth global bleaching event on 15 April 2024. Australia's Great Barrier Reef went through its fifth mass bleaching since 2016, and surveys later found that reefs around Lizard Island and Cooktown had lost more than a third of their live hard coral.

By April 2025, 84 percent of the world's reef area had experienced bleaching-level heat stress, compared with about two-thirds in the previous global event, and mass bleaching had been documented in at least 82 countries and territories. After severe bleaching in Western Australia in early 2025, global heat stress declined. In June 2026 NOAA said the event had most likely ended in mid-2025, while warning that reefs now bleach almost every year and that a developing El Niño could bring another widespread event.

title: Military coup in Myanmar
summary: Myanmar's army detained Aung San Suu Kyi and other elected leaders on 1 February 2021 and seized power, ending a decade of partial civilian rule and setting off mass protests and armed resistance.
body:
In the early hours of 1 February 2021, the day before the newly elected parliament was due to sit, Myanmar's armed forces (the Tatmadaw) detained State Counsellor Aung San Suu Kyi, President Win Myint and other leaders of the governing National League for Democracy (NLD). Acting President Myint Swe declared a one-year state of emergency and handed power to the commander-in-chief, Senior General Min Aung Hlaing.

The military said the November 2020 election, which the NLD had won by a landslide, was marred by fraud, and declared the results invalid; it presented no evidence for the scale of irregularities it alleged. In a statement issued in her name, Aung San Suu Kyi urged people not to accept the takeover. The United States, the United Kingdom and the UN condemned the coup, which came less than ten years after the army had handed power to a civilian government; Myanmar had been under military rule from 1962 to 2011.

The seizure of power was met by mass street protests and a civil disobedience movement. Security forces cracked down on demonstrators, and many protesters later joined armed resistance groups, which, together with long-established ethnic armed organisations, turned the crisis into a nationwide civil war. Aung San Suu Kyi was charged with a series of offences that independent analysts regarded as an attempt to legitimise the takeover.

title: Civil war in Myanmar
summary: A nationwide war between Myanmar's military government and a broad array of armed opponents, triggered by the February 2021 coup and the crackdown on peaceful protests that followed.
body:
The military's seizure of power on 1 February 2021 set off mass demonstrations. After security forces cracked down on them, many protesters sought training from ethnic armed organisations in the borderlands, and the exiled National Unity Government (NUG) formed People's Defence Forces. Insurgencies that had simmered since independence in 1948 merged with a new movement against military rule, and fighting spread to almost every region and state.

From late 2023 the resistance made major gains. Operation 1027, launched by the Three Brotherhood Alliance in northern Shan State in October 2023, set off offensives across the country; rebel forces took the city of Lashio in August 2024, and the Arakan Army captured the army's Western Command headquarters in Rakhine State in December 2024. The military responded with conscription and an intensive air campaign.

Since 2025 the balance has shifted back towards the military, which has relied on mass conscription and air power while its opponents have split into factions: the army retook Kyaukme in October 2025, and the MNDAA withdrew from Lashio under Chinese pressure. The junta held a staged election from December 2025 to January 2026 that UN experts dismissed as a sham, and Min Aung Hlaing was sworn in as president in April 2026.

The monitoring group ACLED estimated in August 2026 that more than 100,000 people had been killed, and the UN says at least 3.6 million people have been displaced. In October 2026 a UN special rapporteur said at least 8,384 civilians had been killed by the military since the coup and described the human rights situation as catastrophic.

title: Rohingya flee Myanmar to Bangladesh
summary: From August 2017 a Myanmar military campaign in Rakhine State drove more than 700,000 Rohingya Muslims into Bangladesh, where most still live in the world's largest refugee camp while genocide cases proceed.
body:
The Rohingya, a mostly Muslim minority in Myanmar's Rakhine State, have faced persecution since at least the 1970s, and successive Myanmar governments have treated many of them as illegal immigrants. After an army crackdown in late 2016, Rohingya insurgents attacked about 30 police posts on 25 August 2017, and the military responded with what it called clearance operations.

According to UN reports, more than 700,000 people fled or were driven into neighbouring Bangladesh by September 2018, the largest exodus in Asia since the Indochina refugee crisis. At least 6,700 Rohingya are estimated to have been killed in the first month alone. UN agencies, human rights groups and several governments accused the military of ethnic cleansing and genocide, including mass killings, sexual violence and the burning of villages; Myanmar's government dismissed the findings as exaggerated.

Most refugees live in camps around Kutupalong in Cox's Bazar district, described as the world's largest refugee settlement. Bangladesh and Myanmar agreed on repatriation in 2017, but the UN says any return must be voluntary and dignified. Since 2024 the Arakan Army, which now controls much of Rakhine State, has also been accused of abuses against Rohingya.

The Gambia brought a genocide case against Myanmar at the International Court of Justice in 2019, which is still being heard, and in 2025 a court in Argentina issued arrest warrants for Myanmar leaders under universal jurisdiction. Aid cuts in 2025 raised fears of hunger in the camps.

title: Taliban return to power in Afghanistan
summary: The Taliban captured Kabul on 15 August 2021 as US-led forces withdrew, restoring their Islamic Emirate and imposing sweeping restrictions on women and girls; only Russia has recognised their government.
body:
Under a February 2020 deal with the Taliban, the United States agreed to withdraw its troops from Afghanistan. As the withdrawal went ahead in 2021, a Taliban offensive that began in May took most provinces in quick succession. On 15 August 2021 Taliban fighters entered Kabul, President Ashraf Ghani fled the country and the Islamic Republic collapsed. Between 14 and 30 August the US and its partners airlifted more than 123,000 people out of Kabul airport; the last US troops left on 30 August, ending almost 20 years of war.

The Taliban restored the Islamic Emirate under their supreme leader, Hibatullah Akhundzada, and named a caretaker government in September 2021. After initially letting women attend university in segregated classes, they barred girls from school beyond the age of 12, banned women from universities in December 2022, excluded them from most jobs, required face coverings in public, limited their travel without a male relative and closed beauty salons, gyms and parks to them. The UN has said the policy of strict separation may amount to gender apartheid.

No government recognised the Taliban until Russia did so in July 2025; the UN has said recognition is impossible while restrictions on women's education and work remain. The country has also suffered a deadly earthquake in Kunar province in 2025 and armed clashes with Pakistan over Pakistani Taliban militants based in Afghanistan.

title: Student-led uprising topples Sheikh Hasina in Bangladesh
summary: Protests against job quotas in Bangladesh grew into a nationwide uprising in July 2024; after a crackdown the UN says killed up to 1,400 people, Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina resigned and fled to India on 5 August.
body:
In June 2024 a court decision reinstated a system reserving 30% of government jobs for descendants of fighters in the 1971 independence war. University students, led by the group Students Against Discrimination, began protesting. The movement intensified in July after Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina referred to the protesters as "grandchildren of Razakars", a highly offensive term for those who collaborated with Pakistan in 1971. Security forces and activists of the ruling Awami League cracked down on them.

The Supreme Court cut the quotas sharply on 21 July, but protesters kept demanding justice for those killed and, on 3 August, Hasina's resignation. On 5 August 2024 Hasina resigned and fled to India by helicopter, ending more than 15 years in power, as crowds celebrated in the streets of Dhaka and stormed her official residence. Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus was sworn in as head of an interim government three days later.

A UN human rights investigation found in February 2025 that as many as 1,400 people may have been killed over 46 days, most of them shot by security forces, and that top leaders directed the repression. In November 2025 a Bangladeshi tribunal sentenced Hasina to death in absentia for crimes against humanity; she rejected the verdict as politically motivated, and the UN reiterated its opposition to the death penalty. In the general election of February 2026, from which the Awami League was barred, the Bangladesh Nationalist Party won a two-thirds majority.

title: Catastrophic monsoon floods in Pakistan
summary: Extreme monsoon rains and glacial melt flooded large parts of Pakistan from June to October 2022, killing 1,739 people and causing about US$40 billion in damage, one of the costliest natural disasters on record.
body:
From mid-June 2022 Pakistan was hit by far heavier monsoon rains than usual, following record-breaking heat waves in May and June that also caused glacial flooding in the north. Climate change minister Sherry Rehman said Sindh and Balochistan received 784% and 500% more rain than their August average. Flash floods and landslides along the Indus and Kabul rivers hit Sindh and Balochistan hardest, along with mountainous areas of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The government declared a state of emergency on 25 August, and Rehman said that a third of the country was under water.

In all, 1,739 people were killed, including 647 children, more than 12,800 were injured and over 2.1 million left homeless. Damage was estimated at about US$40 billion.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said Pakistan, which produces less than 1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, was not to blame for a disaster driven by the climate crisis, and UN Secretary-General António Guterres described it as a "monsoon on steroids". A study by an international team of climate scientists found that global heating had made the flooding up to 50% worse, while unregulated construction and deforestation also worsened the floods.

title: Japan releases treated Fukushima water into the Pacific
summary: Since August 2023 Japan has been discharging treated and diluted water from the wrecked Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant into the Pacific, a process expected to take decades and opposed by China and many in the region.
body:
The 2011 earthquake and tsunami caused meltdowns in three reactors at the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant. Water used to cool the melted fuel, together with groundwater and rain that reached it, became radioactive. The plant's operator, TEPCO, stored it in tanks after treating it with a filtering system that removes most radioactive substances except tritium, which cannot be separated from water. By 2023 the tanks held about 1.34 million tonnes, and more water was being added every day.

Japan's government approved a plan in April 2021 to dilute the treated water with seawater and release it gradually into the ocean. The International Atomic Energy Agency found in 2023 that the plan was consistent with international safety standards and said the radiological impact on people and the environment would be negligible, while stressing that the release was Japan's national decision. Japan's fishing industry, China, South Korea and environmental campaigners opposed it, and trust in TEPCO and the government was low after earlier scandals.

Discharges began on 24 August 2023 and are expected to continue for more than 30 years. China banned imports of Japanese seafood the same day. No elevated tritium levels had been detected in nearby waters by March 2024, and Chinese institutions said in 2025 that their own sampling found no abnormalities. In November 2025, amid a wider diplomatic dispute with Japan, China again halted seafood imports, citing the need to monitor testing of the treated water.

title: Yoon Suk Yeol declares martial law in South Korea
summary: South Korea's president declared martial law on 3 December 2024; parliament voted it down within hours, and Yoon Suk Yeol was impeached, removed from office and later jailed for life for leading an insurrection.
body:
On the night of 3 December 2024, President Yoon Suk Yeol declared emergency martial law in a televised address, accusing the opposition Democratic Party, which controlled the National Assembly, of "anti-state activities" and of collaborating with North Korea. The decree suspended political activity and placed restrictions on the press, and Yoon ordered the arrest of political opponents, including the leader of his own People Power Party. It was the first declaration of martial law since the military dictatorship of Chun Doo-hwan in 1980.

Soldiers were sent to the National Assembly, but 190 legislators made their way in and, shortly after 1 a.m. on 4 December, unanimously voted to lift martial law; Yoon's cabinet lifted it a few hours later. Protests and calls for his resignation followed. The Assembly impeached Yoon on 14 December, suspending him from office. After a failed attempt to detain him in early January, he was arrested on 15 January 2025, the first sitting South Korean president to be arrested, and was indicted for leading an insurrection.

On 4 April 2025 the Constitutional Court unanimously upheld the impeachment and removed Yoon from office. An early presidential election on 3 June 2025 was won by the Democratic Party's Lee Jae Myung. On 19 February 2026 a Seoul court found Yoon guilty of leading an insurrection and sentenced him to life in prison; former defence minister Kim Yong-hyun received 30 years.

title: China–Philippines confrontations at Second Thomas Shoal
summary: Since 2023 Chinese coast guard ships have repeatedly blocked, rammed and fired water cannon at Philippine missions resupplying a grounded warship on Second Thomas Shoal, making the reef a flashpoint in the South China Sea dispute.
body:
Second Thomas Shoal, known as Ayungin in the Philippines and Ren'ai Jiao in China, is a submerged reef in the Spratly Islands about 194 km west of the Philippine island of Palawan. In 1999, after China occupied nearby Mischief Reef, the Philippine Navy deliberately ran aground an old warship, the BRP Sierra Madre, on the shoal; a small detachment of marines has been stationed on the rusting hulk ever since. China claims the reef and has demanded the ship's removal. In 2016 an international arbitral tribunal ruled that the shoal is a low-tide elevation that cannot generate territorial waters of its own.

Under President Rodrigo Duterte the Philippines had accepted an informal understanding with China to keep the status quo, including not reinforcing the ship. His successor, Ferdinand Marcos Jr., said in 2023 that he knew of no such agreement and that if one existed he rescinded it. Confrontations escalated: from August 2023 Chinese coast guard ships used water cannon against Philippine resupply boats and collided with Philippine vessels, and in June 2024 a Philippine sailor was injured in a clash in which, according to the Philippine military, Chinese personnel boarded supply boats.

The Philippines protested the actions as dangerous, while China said it was safeguarding its sovereignty. A provisional arrangement on resupply missions agreed in July 2024 was intended to defuse tensions, but the dispute continues; in April 2026 the Philippines accused Chinese vessels of using cyanide near the reef, a claim Beijing dismissed.

title: Earthquake strikes Japan's Noto Peninsula
summary: A magnitude 7.5 earthquake struck the Noto Peninsula on New Year's Day 2024, triggering a tsunami and fires; 732 deaths were confirmed, the most in a Japanese earthquake since 2016.
body:
At 16:10 local time on 1 January 2024, a shallow earthquake struck near Suzu on the Noto Peninsula in Ishikawa Prefecture, on Japan's Sea of Japan coast. The US Geological Survey measured it at magnitude 7.5 (the Japan Meteorological Agency gave 7.6), and shaking reached the top of Japan's intensity scale. It prompted Japan's first major tsunami warning since the 2011 Tōhoku disaster, with warnings along the west coast and as far as South Korea.

The shaking, tsunami and fires caused widespread destruction in Suzu, Wajima, Noto and Anamizu, with damage also in Toyama and Niigata prefectures; fire destroyed the area around Wajima's morning market. More than 200,000 buildings were damaged across nine prefectures. In all, 732 deaths were confirmed: 228 directly caused by the earthquake and 504 later deaths linked to its aftermath, such as evacuation and outages of power and water. It was Japan's deadliest earthquake since the 2016 Kumamoto earthquake.

The earthquake also deformed the land: GPS measurements showed that the land rose by more than four metres in places and shifted sideways by more than a metre.

title: George Floyd protests
summary: The killing of George Floyd by a Minneapolis police officer in May 2020 set off protests against police brutality and racism across the United States and in dozens of other countries.
body:
On 25 May 2020 George Floyd, a 46-year-old Black man, died during an arrest in Minneapolis after officer Derek Chauvin knelt on his neck for more than nine minutes while three other officers stood by. Bystander video of the arrest spread quickly, and protests began the next day at the intersection of East 38th Street and Chicago Avenue, where he had been detained.

The demonstrations spread to every US state and Washington, D.C., and, according to Wikipedia's summary of the research, to more than 2,000 cities and towns in over 60 countries. Polls cited there estimated that 15 to 26 million people in the US took part at some point in the summer of 2020, which would make them the largest protests in the country's history. The BBC noted that the crowds were more racially mixed than in earlier protests over police killings.

Most protests were peaceful: the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project estimated that 93% of them involved no violence or destruction. Some cities saw arson and looting, which caused an estimated $1–2 billion in insured damage. More than 200 cities imposed curfews, tens of thousands of National Guard members were deployed, and at least 14,000 people had been arrested by the end of June 2020.

The protests prompted police reform proposals at city and state level, though no federal reform bill became law, as well as debates about "defunding" the police and a wave of monument removals and renamings. In April 2021 a jury convicted Chauvin of murder and manslaughter; he was sentenced to 22.5 years in prison.

title: Supporters of Donald Trump attack the US Capitol
summary: On 6 January 2021 a mob of Donald Trump's supporters stormed the US Capitol to try to stop Congress from certifying Joe Biden's victory in the 2020 presidential election.
body:
Two months after losing the 2020 presidential election, Donald Trump continued to claim falsely that the vote had been stolen. Thousands of his supporters gathered in Washington, D.C., on 6 January 2021, the day Congress met to count the Electoral College votes. At a rally near the White House, Trump repeated his claims and urged the crowd to "fight like hell".

Thousands then marched to the Capitol, and hundreds broke through police lines. The FBI estimates that 2,000 to 2,500 people entered the building, where some vandalised offices and assaulted police officers and journalists. Members of Congress were evacuated and both chambers were locked down. The building was cleared by the evening, and the count resumed and was completed early on 7 January, confirming Biden's victory.

According to Wikipedia's account of official figures, five people died within 36 hours, including a rioter shot by Capitol Police and an officer who died of a stroke the day after being assaulted; at least 174 police officers were injured, and four officers who responded later died by suicide. Members of the Proud Boys and Oath Keepers took part, and several were later convicted of seditious conspiracy.

The House impeached Trump for incitement of insurrection a week later; in February 2021 the Senate voted 57–43 to convict him, ten votes short of the two-thirds needed. A House select committee investigated the attack, and Trump was later indicted over efforts to overturn the election, but those charges were dismissed after he won the 2024 election. On 20 January 2025, his first day back in office, Trump granted clemency to about 1,200 people convicted over the attack and ended the remaining cases.

title: Gang violence and political crisis in Haiti
summary: Since the assassination of President Jovenel Moïse in July 2021, armed gangs have taken control of much of Haiti's capital while the country has had no elected president and repeated attempts at an international security force.
body:
Haiti's crisis began with protests over fuel prices and corruption in 2018 and deepened sharply on 7 July 2021, when President Jovenel Moïse was killed at his residence, allegedly by a group of foreign mercenaries. Ariel Henry, whom Moïse had named prime minister days earlier, took office on 20 July promising to restore security and hold long-delayed elections, which did not take place.

Armed gangs, some with ties to politicians and business figures according to UN and Canadian investigations cited by Wikipedia, expanded their control over the capital, blockading the main fuel terminal in 2022. In March 2024, while Henry was abroad, gangs tried to seize the capital's airport to stop him from returning; the UN human rights chief said 1,193 people had been killed by gang violence since the start of that year. Henry resigned in April 2024 and a nine-member transitional presidential council took power.

A Kenya-led multinational police mission authorised by the UN in 2023 struggled with a lack of funding and personnel. In September 2025 the UN Security Council voted to replace it with a larger Gang Suppression Force of up to 5,550 personnel. The transitional council's mandate ended on 7 February 2026 and Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé took over executive power. The first troops of the new force, from Chad, arrived in April 2026.

The violence has killed thousands of people and displaced more than a million, according to Al Jazeera. Haiti has not held an election since 2016; votes planned for 2026 were postponed, and in October 2026 authorities postponed indefinitely the elections due in December.

title: Venezuela's disputed 2024 election and its aftermath
summary: Nicolás Maduro claimed victory in Venezuela's July 2024 presidential election despite opposition tallies showing he lost; the dispute led to a crackdown, US military pressure and, in January 2026, Maduro's capture by US forces.
body:
Venezuela held a presidential election on 28 July 2024. The government barred the main opposition leader, María Corina Machado, from running, and former diplomat Edmundo González stood instead. The government-controlled National Electoral Council declared Nicolás Maduro the winner without publishing detailed results, while the opposition published polling-station tallies that it said showed González had won by a wide margin. The Carter Center, the Organization of American States and the United Nations rejected the official result, and governments from Washington to Santiago questioned it.

Protests followed and the government launched a crackdown; The New York Times reported at least 22 deaths and more than 2,000 people jailed within days. On 22 August the Supreme Tribunal of Justice endorsed Maduro's victory. González, facing an arrest warrant, went into exile in Spain in September, and Maduro was sworn in for a third term on 10 January 2025. Machado, who stayed in hiding, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in October 2025.

From September 2025 the United States built up warships in the Caribbean and struck dozens of boats it said were carrying drugs, killing more than 100 people, according to US announcements reported by the Associated Press. On 3 January 2026 US forces struck targets in Venezuela and captured Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, who were flown to New York to face drug-trafficking charges; they pleaded not guilty. UN officials and many legal experts said the raid violated the UN Charter.

Vice-president Delcy Rodríguez was sworn in as acting president on 5 January 2026. Her government restored relations with Washington, opened the oil sector to private companies and passed an amnesty law under which hundreds of political prisoners were released. Maduro's trial in New York has been scheduled for June 2027.
