title: Bolsonaro supporters storm Brazil's seats of power in Brasília
summary: On 8 January 2023, a week after Lula took office, supporters of defeated president Jair Bolsonaro stormed Brazil's Congress, Supreme Court and presidential palace, calling for the military to intervene.
body:
Jair Bolsonaro lost Brazil's October 2022 presidential election to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Many of his supporters claimed, without evidence, that the electronic vote had been rigged; the armed forces, which helped oversee the election, found no sign of fraud. For weeks afterwards supporters blocked roads and camped outside army barracks, and Bolsonaro's allies had floated the idea of an assault like the 6 January 2021 attack on the US Capitol.

On 8 January 2023, a week after Lula's inauguration, thousands of Bolsonaro supporters, about 3,000 according to Brazilian media cited by Al Jazeera, broke into the National Congress, the Supreme Federal Court and the Planalto presidential palace on Brasília's Three Powers Square. They smashed windows and furniture and unfurled a banner reading "intervention" on the roof of Congress, an appeal for the military to overturn the result. Neither Lula nor Bolsonaro, who was in Florida, was in the capital. Security forces took more than five hours to clear the buildings.

Lula signed a decree placing the Federal District under a federal state of emergency until the end of January and vowed to punish those responsible. Police arrested about 300 people that day, and the Supreme Court suspended the Federal District's governor, Ibaneis Rocha, for 90 days for failing to prevent the riot. More than 1,400 people were later charged over the attacks.

Investigations into the riots and the weeks before them uncovered what prosecutors described as a plot to keep Bolsonaro in power. In September 2025 the Supreme Federal Court convicted Bolsonaro of attempting a coup and sentenced him to 27 years and 3 months in prison.

title: Ecuador's "internal armed conflict" against drug gangs
summary: In January 2024 Ecuador's president declared an internal armed conflict against drug-trafficking gangs after a prison escape and a wave of attacks; the military campaign continues while homicides have kept rising.
body:
Ecuador, between the world's two largest cocaine producers, Colombia and Peru, became a major transit route for the drug in the 2010s. Gangs such as Los Choneros and Los Lobos fought over routes, prisons and the port of Guayaquil, and the homicide rate rose from 5 to 46 per 100,000 people between 2017 and 2023, according to figures cited by Wikipedia.

On 7 January 2024 Adolfo Macías, known as "Fito", the leader of Los Choneros, escaped from prison in Guayaquil. President Daniel Noboa declared a state of emergency, and gangs responded with riots in several prisons, where more than 130 guards and staff were taken hostage, and with bombings and kidnappings. On 9 January gunmen stormed a television studio in Guayaquil during a live broadcast. Noboa then declared an "internal armed conflict", designated 22 gangs as terrorist organisations and ordered the military to "neutralise" them.

The campaign brought mass arrests, more than 31,000 by late 2025 according to Wikipedia, and Fito was recaptured in June 2025 and extradited to the United States. But violence grew: Ecuador recorded an estimated 9,216 murders in 2025, more than 30% up on the previous year, according to Al Jazeera. In November 2025 voters rejected Noboa's proposal to allow foreign military bases, but from March 2026 US forces supported Ecuadorian strikes against gangs inside the country.

title: Mexican drug war
summary: Since December 2006 Mexico's government has used the army and police against drug cartels; the cartels splintered and fought each other, and the conflict has killed well over 100,000 people.
body:
Mexican trafficking groups grew powerful in the 1990s after the fall of the Colombian Medellín and Cali cartels. On 11 December 2006 President Felipe Calderón launched Operation Michoacán, the first of militarised campaigns that sent tens of thousands of soldiers and federal police against the cartels in Michoacán, Ciudad Juárez, Tijuana and Tamaulipas.

The arrests and killings of leaders split the cartels into smaller, often more violent factions that fought over territory. By the end of Calderón's term in 2012 the official death toll was at least 60,000, and some estimates exceeded 120,000 dead by 2013, besides tens of thousands missing, according to figures compiled by Wikipedia. Security forces were accused of extrajudicial killings, torture and disappearances, and the 2014 disappearance of 43 students in Iguala, in which local police were implicated, became a symbol of collusion and impunity.

Andrés Manuel López Obrador, president from 2018, promised "hugs, not bullets", focusing on social programmes, and declared the war over in 2019, but he kept the military in policing through a new National Guard. A failed attempt to arrest a son of the jailed Sinaloa cartel leader Joaquín "El Chapo" Guzmán in Culiacán that year ended with the suspect released to stop the fighting. The Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) expanded rapidly.

President Claudia Sheinbaum, in office since 2024, has largely continued that strategy while making greater use of intelligence and targeted operations, as the Trump administration pressed Mexico to crack down on the cartels. In February 2026 the army killed the CJNG's leader, Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, "El Mencho", setting off blockades and burning vehicles across much of the country.

title: Wildfires devastate the Los Angeles area
summary: In January 2025 wind-driven wildfires, above all the Palisades and Eaton fires, swept through parts of Los Angeles, killing at least 31 people and destroying around 20,000 homes and other buildings.
body:
Between 7 and 31 January 2025, 14 destructive wildfires burned in the Los Angeles area and San Diego County. They were driven by Santa Ana winds that in places reached 100 miles per hour (160 km/h), after months without rain had dried out vegetation that had grown thickly during two very wet winters. Scientists quoted by the BBC said climate change had made such swings between wet and dry conditions more common, raising the fire risk.

The two largest fires broke out on 7 January. The Palisades Fire erupted in Pacific Palisades, a neighbourhood east of Malibu, and the Eaton Fire, which started that evening in the foothills of the Angeles National Forest, swept into Altadena. More than 200,000 people were ordered to evacuate. Ground crews and firefighting aircraft fought the fires for more than three weeks until both were declared fully contained on 31 January.

According to Wikipedia's summary of official figures, the fires killed at least 31 people, destroyed around 20,000 homes and other structures and burned more than 57,000 acres. The Palisades and Eaton fires were likely the second- and third-most destructive in California's history. A study published in August 2025 linked up to 440 deaths to the fires, including indirect ones.

In October 2025 federal authorities arrested a 29-year-old man and charged him with starting the Palisades Fire. Prosecutors allege that he set a small fire on 1 January, the Lachman Fire, which was put out but kept smouldering underground before being rekindled by the winds on 7 January.

title: Hunga Tonga–Hunga Haʻapai volcano erupts and sends a tsunami across the Pacific
summary: On 15 January 2022 an undersea volcano in Tonga produced the largest atmospheric explosion ever recorded by modern instruments, triggering tsunamis that devastated parts of Tonga and reached coasts around the Pacific.
body:
Hunga Tonga–Hunga Haʻapai, a submarine volcano about 65 km north of Tonga's main island, Tongatapu, began erupting on 20 December 2021. After a lull, it exploded with great force at about 5 p.m. local time on 15 January 2022, sending gas and ash about 58 km high, into the mesosphere. According to Wikipedia's summary of the research, it was the largest volcanic eruption since Mount Pinatubo in 1991 and the largest explosion in the atmosphere recorded by modern instruments; the blast was heard more than 2,000 km away in New Zealand.

The eruption set off tsunamis that, according to the US Geological Survey, reached as high as 65 feet (20 m) on Tongan islands, destroyed hundreds of structures, displaced more than 1,500 people and killed four people in Tonga. Waves also crossed the Pacific: two people drowned in Peru, where the tsunami also caused an oil spill, and damage was reported in Fiji, Hawaii, Chile, California, Japan, Russia and New Zealand.

Tonga's government called it an "unprecedented disaster". Every house on Mango Island was destroyed, and ash covered Tongatapu. Damage to submarine cables caused communication outages, and in the first days the UN said it had not been possible to contact the Haʻapai and Vavaʻu island groups.

Scientists were surprised that the eruption produced both ordinary tsunamis, caused by displaced water, and fast-moving "meteotsunamis" driven by the pressure wave in the atmosphere. The USGS said the relatively low death toll was helped by warnings and Tonga's long-standing practice of tsunami drills.

title: Unrest in New Caledonia over voting reform
summary: In May 2024 riots broke out in the French Pacific territory of New Caledonia over a reform that would have let more recent arrivals vote in local elections, which Indigenous Kanak independence supporters said would dilute their voice.
body:
Under the 1998 Nouméa Accord, which followed violent clashes in the 1980s, the right to vote in New Caledonia's provincial elections and independence referendums was limited to people living there before 1998 and their descendants. By 2023 about one in five national voters in the territory was excluded. Three referendums, the last in 2021, rejected independence, but most independence supporters boycotted the last one, held during the COVID-19 pandemic, and rejected its legitimacy. In 2024 the French government moved to change the constitution to open the local electorate to people resident for ten years.

On 13 May 2024, as the National Assembly in Paris debated the reform, protests in and around the capital, Nouméa, turned into riots. Businesses were burned and looted, and parts of the city and its suburbs became no-go zones. France declared a state of emergency on 16 May, banned TikTok, imposed a curfew and sent about 3,000 soldiers and police. It was the territory's deadliest unrest in four decades, according to AFP: at least 13 people were killed, hundreds were injured, and damage was estimated at €1.5 billion.

President Emmanuel Macron visited on 22 May and later suspended the reform after calling snap elections; in October Prime Minister Michel Barnier dropped it. Pro-independence leader Christian Tein and ten others were arrested in June on suspicion of instigating the violence. The curfew was lifted on 2 December 2024. In July 2025 France and New Caledonian politicians agreed in principle that the territory would become a "State of New Caledonia" within the French Republic.
